property_summary: For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner getter equals the supplied newOwner; the mutant resets owner to address(0) so this property is violated for some newOwner values.

If a call to transferOwnership is made by the current owner to set a new owner X, then afterwards the contract's owner getter must equal X; the mutant that resets owner to address(0) breaks this for some X.

For any caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner != address(0), after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() getter must return the supplied newOwner; the mutant that resets owner to address(0) violates this when newOwner != address(0).

For any caller that is the current owner and any candidate newOwner (including address(0)), after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner() getter reflects the final stored owner; the correct contract sets owner to newOwner, while the buggy mutant sometimes leaves owner != newOwner (specifically it becomes address(0)).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and afterwards the contract's owner() is nonzero iff the provided newOwner is nonzero — the reference sets owner to newOwner while the mutant always resets owner to address(0), so there exist inputs (any nonzero newOwner) where the mutant leaves owner()==address(0) but the reference leaves owner()==newOwner.

The owner-only modifier prevents non-owner addresses from calling owned(): for every caller address, if it's not the contract owner then calling owned() must not change the owner (only the owner can call it to affect ownership); the mutant removes that restriction so some non-owner caller can call owned() and cause owner to differ afterwards.

For every caller address, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner when the caller is not the current owner; the mutant removes the ownership restriction allowing some non-owner caller to execute owned() and thereby change owner for some input.

For every caller address and any attempted newOwner address, calling transferOwnership via the onlyOwner-protected owned() entrypoint cannot change owner unless the caller is the current owner; the mutant removes the require and thus allows some non-owner caller (fuzzer-found) to change owner via owned(), violating that rule.

For every caller address, calling owned() cannot change the contract's owner (the owner() getter remains equal to the pre-call owner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction so some caller can call owned() and change owner, violating this invariant.

For every caller address, calling owned() does not change the contract's owner (owner stays equal to the pre-call owner) — the mutant removes the onlyOwner restriction allowing some caller to change owner via owned(), violating this invariant.

For any caller who is the current owner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner must equal the supplied newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender and thus can violate this when owner transfers to any address != msg.sender.

For any caller that is the current owner and any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner becomes exactly the provided newOwner; the mutant instead sets owner to msg.sender and thus can differ when newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller who is the current owner and any candidate newOwner (any address), after transferOwnership(newOwner) completes the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner; the mutant instead assigns msg.sender, so when owner calls transferOwnership with newOwner != msg.sender the mutant breaks the rule.

For any caller who is the current owner and any address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner; the mutant sets owner to msg.sender and thus violates this when newOwner != msg.sender.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address newOwner, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's owner equals the provided newOwner; the mutant assigns owner = msg.sender instead, so when newOwner != msg.sender the mutant breaks this rule.

For any caller that is the current owner and any newOwner address, after calling transferOwnership(newOwner) the contract's public owner must equal newOwner; the mutant that removes the assignment breaks this because owner will not update for some inputs.

For all callers, only the account stored in C.owner can successfully call transferOwnership (i.e., transferOwnership always updates owner only when tx.sender == owner); the mutant replacing msg.sender with tx.origin allows a contract caller to bypass owner checks when the contract is called via another EOA, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For any caller address A and newOwner address N, only calls where msg.sender == c.owner can change c.owner (i.e., transferOwnership succeeds only when the direct caller is the stored owner); the mutant using tx.origin allows a contract intermediary to change owner when the origin EOA equals owner but the direct caller is a contract, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every admissible input, only an EOA that is the direct caller (msg.sender) equal to C.owner can successfully change owner via transferOwnership; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows an intermediary contract caller to change owner when tx.origin == owner, violating this rule for some inputs.

For all calls to transferOwnership routed through a CALLER contract, the reference requires the direct caller (msg.sender) to equal owner so only the deployed owner-contract can transfer ownership; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows an intermediary contract caller to transfer ownership when tx.origin==owner (but msg.sender!=owner), so there exist inputs (an owner EOA and a caller contract) that make the mutant change owner while the reference forbids it.

For every admissible inputs: only a direct call whose msg.sender equals C.owner can successfully change owner via transferOwnership; the mutant that checks tx.origin instead allows an intermediary contract caller (msg.sender != owner but tx.origin == owner) to change owner, violating this rule for some inputs.
